units.title: Privacy, confidentiality and disclosure
units.content: Under Australia's Privacy Act framework, secondary disclosure needs consent or an applicable exception. Serious-threat disclosure requires a reasonable belief in necessity and consent being unreasonable or impracticable to obtain. Additional state or territory rules may apply.

source.jurisdiction: Australia; entities covered by the Privacy Act
source.excerpt: Chapter 3: secondary purpose; Serious threat. Short anchor: 'unreasonable or impracticable'.
source.limitation: Permission is not a universal duty to disclose; local law and confidentiality obligations still require checking.

units.title: Children, consent and parental access
units.content: OAIC health-record guidance distinguishes children who can make their own access request from those who need a parent or guardian to act for them. Where the child has capacity, the parent should ordinarily be advised that the child needs to make the request.

source.jurisdiction: Australia; Privacy Act health information access
source.limitation: Health-record access guidance, not a universal rule for treatment consent, parental rights or mandatory reporting.

units.title: Decision-making capacity and supported consent
units.content: RANZCP ethics guidance for psychiatry recognises that capacity can vary with the decision and fluctuate over time. It supports assisting the person's own decision-making and considering their wishes when substitute consent is necessary.

source.limitation: Does not establish a legal incompetence test, guardianship authority or a jurisdiction-specific substitute decision hierarchy.

units.title: Clinical expertise, referral and continuity
units.content: RANZCP guidance asks psychiatrists to recognise expertise limits and consult suitable colleagues when needed. It also supports coordinated care and suitable alternative arrangements when a referral is declined.

source.limitation: Does not prove any particular specialist's competence, availability or suitability; no medication or referral eligibility protocol.

units.title: Forensic assessment purpose and unbiased diagnosis
units.content: For Australian doctors conducting third-party medico-legal assessments, the usual therapeutic relationship does not apply. Medical Board guidance requires explaining the assessment role and purpose and providing an impartial report. This does not determine a court's competency or custody test.

source.limitation: Doctor-specific professional guidance, not a jurisdiction-specific competency test or direct regulation of psychologists.

units.title: Religious preferences and treatment discussions
units.content: RANZCP psychiatry guidance respects religion and patient preferences while permitting refusal of harmful or unhelpful treatment. Consent discussions include risks and alternatives; this does not establish that a fasting-related medication change is safe.

source.limitation: No dosing recommendation, guarantee about fasting or treatment exemption; patient-specific prescribing assessment remains necessary.

units.title: Accurate clinical records, diagnosis and reports
units.content: Australian medical guidance calls for accurate clinical records covering findings, diagnosis and management. Reports and certificates require reasonable verification, honesty and stated knowledge limits; relevant information should not be deliberately omitted to achieve a desired outcome.

source.limitation: Professional standard for doctors, not a claim that it directly regulates psychologists or determines any court or workplace outcome.

units.title: Financial interests and competing professional roles
units.content: Medical Board guidance for Australian doctors requires identifying and managing interests that could compromise care, including perceived conflicts. Referrals should serve patients' interests; commercial arrangements must not adversely influence treatment.

source.limitation: No automatic finding of bribery, misconduct or mandatory reporting; specific duties depend on the facts and applicable law.

units.title: Cultural safety and individual preferences
units.content: Australian medical guidance emphasises self-determined healthcare, respect for cultural and religious diversity, and avoiding stereotypes. Cultural safety depends on the individual's experience; respecting culture does not require providing unsafe or inappropriate care.

source.limitation: Does not require automatically involving family, an interpreter or cultural liaison against an individual's wishes; assess communication needs individually.

units.title: Workplace assessment and disability adjustments
units.content: Australian Human Rights Commission guidance focuses on actual ability to perform a job's inherent requirements, rather than disability stereotypes. Adjustments can support that ability; unjustifiable hardship is a qualified exception that requires consideration and discussion.

source.limitation: Not a case-specific fitness clearance, employment law opinion or exhaustive account of discrimination exceptions.

units.title: Individual care planning and follow-up
units.content: Australia's comprehensive-care standard supports assessment and an individual plan developed with the patient: agreed goals, chosen support people, appropriate follow-up referrals, and review when needs change. A plan should reflect available evidence and the patient's preferences.

source.publisher: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
source.limitation: Organisational care standard, not a legal discharge test, prescribing authority or guarantee of service availability.

units.title: Sexual orientation, gender and non-coercive care
units.content: RANZCP opposes conversion practices intended to change or suppress sexual orientation or gender identity, citing potential harm. Family or religious pressure does not make such a practice a supported therapeutic goal.

source.limitation: Professional opposition, not a statement of the current criminal law or treatment rules in every jurisdiction.

units.title: Australian crisis support
units.content: In Australia, Lifeline offers crisis support by phone at 13 11 14, available around the clock. If life is in danger, call 000. These contacts do not replace an individual assessment or establish confidentiality guarantees.

source.excerpt: Get Help and What we do: 'If life is in danger, call 000'.
source.limitation: Only selected for safety-relevant questions; no promise about anonymity, confidentiality exceptions, response time or clinical treatment.

units.title: Perspective for care discussion
units.content: Questions about your care goals, available choices and preferred support people can guide discussion.

source.publisher: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
source.excerpt: Action 5.13; role-framing paraphrase of patient goals and desired support participation.
source.limitation: Harmless communication framing; creates no professional authority or factual entitlement.

units.title: Perspective for care discussion
units.content: Support can be discussed around the person's own goals and preferences, including whom they want involved.

source.publisher: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
source.excerpt: Action 5.13; role-framing paraphrase of patient goals and desired support participation.
source.limitation: Harmless communication framing; creates no professional authority or factual entitlement.

units.title: Perspective for care discussion
units.content: Organise the care discussion around assessed needs, shared goals and appropriate follow-up.
